record.narrative: This first registration wave prioritizes high-confidence biomarker-to-dependency relationships in the supplied lung cell-line CRISPR screen dataset. For MAPK/RAS-related oncogenic drivers, I test the expected selective dependency: KRAS mutations should associate with stronger KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E with stronger BRAF dependency; EGFR amplification with stronger EGFR dependency; and ERBB2 amplification with stronger ERBB2 dependency. For chromatin and DNA-repair dependencies, SMARCA4 loss is a canonical context for SMARCA2 dependency, and MSI-high is a strong context for WRN dependency. For MDM2 and USP7, I compare TP53 wild-type (tp53_loss=0) versus TP53 loss (tp53_loss=1), with the hypothesis that wild-type TP53 cells may show stronger dependency on p53-pathway regulators through USP7-MDM2-p53 circuitry, although direction is left as a testable hypothesis. MYC amplification is used for broad transcription/translation-associated dependencies (POLR2A, RPL11, DHX9), based on the prior that MYC-driven cells have heightened transcriptional and ribosome-biogenesis demands. KEAP1 loss is tested against NFE2L2 dependency because loss of KEAP1 activates NRF2/NFE2L2 pathway signaling and may alter selective dependency. All proposed comparisons are pre-registered as unresolved, because no dataset evidence has yet been returned. The direction is coded as -1 because more negative dependency scores mean stronger dependency; the expected raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast is negative under the proposed biology. A signed estimate will support stronger dependency when it is positive under this coding. I will assess both the magnitude relative to the 10% threshold and the 95% Welch uncertainty, while keeping claims limited to associations in this dataset.

No claims currently have direct evidence. I will request analyses for all 12 newly registered main-effect claims. These cover canonical and high-confidence biological contexts: driver-specific dependencies for KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2; TP53-pathway dependencies for MDM2 and USP7; SMARCA4-loss-associated SMARCA2 dependency; MSI-high-associated WRN dependency; KEAP1-loss-associated NFE2L2 dependency; and MYC-amplification-associated transcription/translation-associated dependencies for RPL11, POLR2A, and DHX9. Selecting all available registered comparisons maximizes the initial evidence needed to distinguish large, precise associations from null or imprecise results. No assessments are due because no evidence has yet been returned.

All 12 discovery results are valid under the 20-observation cell rule and have Welch intervals signed to the registered hypothesis direction. Because direction is -1 for all original claims, a positive signed estimate corresponds to a more negative (stronger) dependency in the exposed group, whereas a negative signed estimate corresponds to weaker dependency. To judge the 10% clinical-significance threshold, I used a rough comparator-mean relative benchmark from the outcome mean and cell proportions. For the main outcomes around -0.25, a 10% threshold is approximately 0.025 dependency-score units; for outcomes with near-zero overall means (NFE2L2 and USP7), relative thresholds must be interpreted carefully, but absolute effects above 0.75 are extremely large and unambiguous. H6 (SMARCA2: SMARCA4 loss vs intact, signed +0.784, 95% CI +0.765 to +0.803) and H7 (WRN: MSI-high vs MSI-low, signed +0.790, CI +0.760 to +0.819) show very large, precise associations in the expected stronger-dependency direction and should be accepted as dataset-supported associations. H12 (USP7: TP53 wild-type vs TP53 loss, signed +0.802, CI +0.782 to +0.822) is also huge and precise, indicating much stronger USP7 dependency in TP53 wild-type cells than in TP53-loss cells; this is accepted as a dataset association, though causal interpretation requires validation and confounding assessment. H8 is opposite to the registered KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2-dependency direction: signed estimate -0.796 (CI -0.816 to -0.776) means KEAP1-loss cells have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency (less negative scores), not stronger; thus H8 is rejected and a reversed claim is registered. H2, H9, H10, and H11 show no clinically meaningful support in the expected direction; their upper signed bounds fall below an approximately 10% threshold, so they are rejected. H1, H3, H4, and H5 remain unresolved because their intervals include both null/contrary effects and values near or above the 10% benchmark. H3 is the strongest unresolved driver-specific effect (EGFR amplification vs EGFR dependency, signed +0.025, CI nearly from 0 to +0.051) and is biologically plausible but imprecise; I request independent validation for H3 because a clean positive result would justify acceptance, while a null or negative validation would justify rejection. Multiple comparisons were considered: the accepted effects are so far beyond uncertainty and the clinical threshold that they are not plausibly explained by 12 tests alone, whereas the borderline effects are being treated conservatively. Current conclusions are limited to this supplied lung-cell-line CRISPR dataset and do not prove causality or generalizability.

Synthesis of iteration 1: the only due response is validation R13 for H3, EGFR amplification versus stronger EGFR dependency. The claim direction is signed so that a positive estimate corresponds to a more negative, stronger dependency in EGFR-amplified cells. Discovery R3 was borderline positive and imprecise, estimate +0.0252 with a 95 percent interval -0.0003 to +0.0507; relative to the comparator mean around -0.25, a 10 percent clinically significant difference is roughly 0.025 dependency-score units. Independent validation R13 was small and opposite to the hypothesis, estimate -0.0070, with a wide independent interval -0.0487 to +0.0347 under the stricter validation alpha. The validation therefore fails to corroborate the borderline discovery effect, and the combined evidence does not support a scientifically meaningful EGFR-amplification association with EGFR dependency in this dataset. I reject H3 and close this specific main-effect claim, but this rejection means the supplied dataset does not support the registered association, not that EGFR amplification can never affect EGFR dependency in other contexts. Overall supported dataset findings are H6 SMARCA4 loss associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, H7 MSI-high associated with stronger WRN dependency, H12 TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss associated with stronger USP7 dependency, and H13 the reversed NFE2L2 claim, where KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker, less negative NFE2L2 dependency rather than stronger dependency. H6, H7, and H12/H13 have huge absolute effects with narrow intervals, far exceeding the relative 10 percent benchmark for outcomes with mean dependency near -0.25; for USP7 and NFE2L2, where overall means are near zero, relative percentage interpretation is less stable, but the absolute effects of about 0.78 to 0.80 dependency-score units are unambiguous within the dataset. Negative or unsupported findings include H2 BRAF V600E versus stronger BRAF dependency, H8 original KEAP1-loss direction for stronger NFE2L2 dependency, H9 through H11 MYC amplification versus stronger RPL11, POLR2A, or DHX9 dependency, and now H3 EGFR amplification versus EGFR dependency after validation. Unresolved uncertainty remains mainly for H1 KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency, H4 ERBB2 amplification versus ERBB2 dependency, and H5 TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss for MDM2 dependency; each has some positive signal but intervals include null and clinically modest effects, so none is accepted. The next most informative analyses should analyze already registered refinements H14 through H23, especially context specificity for the accepted strong effects and the ARID1A-SMARCA2 comparison. If a refined effect is precise, crosses the 10 percent threshold, and is biologically coherent, independent validation would then be useful. All conclusions are limited to associations in the supplied lung cell-line CRISPR dataset and do not establish causality or clinical generalizability.

Iteration 2 explore focuses on three scientific needs: context-specific robustness of the already accepted strong dependency associations, resolution of borderline MAPK driver claims after the initial broad tests, and a small expansion into biologically motivated DNA-repair/chromatin contexts. First, I register main-effect refinements for the accepted strong effects within adenocarcinoma: SMARCA4-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency, TP53 wild-type versus TP53-loss for USP7 dependency, KEAP1-loss versus weaker NFE2L2 dependency under the reversed direction, and MSI-high versus WRN dependency. These are absolute subgroup effect checks rather than interaction tests; they are useful because a large accepted effect could be diluted, concentrated, or absent in the largest lineage subtype. Second, I register pure-context refinements for MAPK dependencies. The broad KRAS and ERBB2 effects remain unresolved, and the broad BRAF test was negative. Excluding alternative MAPK pathway drivers may reveal a cleaner oncogene-selective effect if the prior nulls were diluted by mixed driver biology. This remains hypothesis generation in the supplied dataset, not a causal test. Third, I add an ARID1A-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency test restricted to SMARCA4-intact cells, which asks whether a second BAF subunit loss marks SMARCA2 dependency independently of the canonical SMARCA4-loss context. Finally, I add a technical robustness check for SMARCA4-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency within the dominant Avana library and a biologically motivated WRN context using BRCA2 loss. These proposals are registered as unresolved because they are new comparisons. Direction coding follows the established convention: direction -1 means a positive signed estimate corresponds to a more negative dependency score in the exposed group, while direction +1 means a positive signed estimate corresponds to a less negative/stronger raw score in the exposed group. For NFE2L2, the reversed accepted finding used direction +1 because KEAP1 loss appeared to weaken dependency, so subtype-robustness claims keep that sign.

No evidence assessments are currently due. I selected 12 previously registered analyses to balance robustness checks for the already accepted large dependency associations, follow-up of unresolved biologically coherent predictors, and expansion to several untested outcomes. The first set checks context specificity of accepted effects without relying immediately on interaction tests: adenocarcinoma-restricted SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2, TP53 wild-type/USP7, KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 with the reversed direction, MSI-high/WRN, and an Avana-library restriction for SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2. These are direct absolute effects and should indicate whether the accepted associations are diluted or remain extreme in the largest subtype and the dominant library. Next, ARID1A-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency restricted to SMARCA4-intact cells tests whether a second BAF-associated context marks SMARCA2 dependency independent of canonical SMARCA4 loss, and BRCA2 loss versus WRN tests a DNA-repair context beyond MSI-high status. Third, pure MAPK-driver contexts for KRAS mutation/dependency_KRAS and ERBB2 amplification/dependency_ERBB2 are prioritized to resolve whether prior broad borderline effects were obscured by alternative drivers; pure BRAF context is deferred because BRAF V600E is rarer and the broad claim was negative, so I allocate slots to other high-value comparisons. Finally, adenocarcinoma-restricted TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss for MDM2 addresses the unresolved p53-MDM2 hypothesis, while RB1 loss/KIF18A and KRAS mutation/RIT1 expand coverage to untested outcomes with biologically motivated predictors. Interaction claims such as subtype interactions are not selected now because four-cell interaction analyses are less direct than absolute subgroup claims and may be underpowered for some rare contexts; absolute subgroup analyses can provide clearer effect estimates first.

All 12 new discovery estimates are valid under the cell-count rule and are already signed to their registered hypothesis direction. For direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means stronger, more negative dependency in the exposed group; for H26, direction +1 and positive signed estimate mean a less negative, weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss cells, consistent with the previously accepted reversed direction. I compared each effect against a rough 10% comparator-mean benchmark: outcomes with mean dependency around -0.25 to -0.31 imply absolute thresholds near 0.025 to 0.030, while near-zero outcomes such as USP7 and NFE2L2 should be judged primarily by absolute dependency-score differences because relative percentages become unstable. H24 adenocarcinoma SMARCA4-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency, H25 adenocarcinoma TP53 wild-type versus TP53-loss versus USP7 dependency, H26 adenocarcinoma KEAP1-loss versus weaker NFE2L2 dependency, H27 adenocarcinoma MSI-high versus WRN dependency, and H32 Avana-library SMARCA4-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency all have enormous absolute effects around +0.78 to +0.80 with lower bounds still far above any plausible 10% benchmark. These accept the context-specific extensions of the already supported dataset findings and show that the main effects are not diluted in adenocarcinoma or the dominant Avana library. H31 shows no independent ARID1A-loss association with SMARCA2 dependency among SMARCA4-intact cells: signed estimate -0.003, CI -0.025 to +0.019, so ARID1A is not supported as a separate BAF-loss marker in this dataset. H33 BRCA2-loss versus WRN is essentially null, estimate -0.00008, but the interval is wide because BRCA2 loss is rare and reaches above a possible 10% positive benchmark, so I leave it unresolved but deferred. H28 pure MAPK-driver KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency remains borderline positive but imprecise, estimate +0.013, CI -0.007 to +0.033; excluding BRAF, EGFR, and ERBB2 drivers did not resolve the broader KRAS claim. H30 pure ERBB2 amplification versus ERBB2 dependency is opposite to the expected direction with upper signed bound below the rough 10% benchmark, so I reject that specific claim. H16 adenocarcinoma TP53 wild-type versus TP53-loss for MDM2 is small and imprecise, estimate +0.016, CI -0.014 to +0.046; it supports neither acceptance nor a confident null. H19 RB1-loss versus KIF18A is small positive but imprecise and remains unresolved. H21 KRAS mutation versus RIT1 dependency is small and opposite to expected with upper bound well below the benchmark, so I reject it. The multiple-comparison burden across the first 24 main-effect tests does not credibly explain the very large accepted effects, whereas the small MAPK and MDM2 effects should remain cautious. I request independent validation for H1 broad KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency because it is the most biologically important remaining unresolved driver dependency and pure-context KRAS evidence did not settle it.

Synthesis of validation for H1: broad KRAS mutation versus stronger KRAS dependency. The registered direction is negative for the raw difference, so a positive signed estimate means a more negative, stronger KRAS dependency in KRAS-mutant cells, whereas a negative signed estimate means weaker KRAS dependency in KRAS-mutant cells. Discovery R1 was a small positive but imprecise association, estimate +0.0137 with 95 percent interval -0.0038 to +0.0312. Using the overall dependency_KRAS mean around -0.245, a 10 percent relative clinical benchmark is approximately 0.0245 dependency-score units, so the discovery estimate itself was below the benchmark and only its upper bound crossed it. Independent validation R26 was in the opposite direction, estimate -0.0152, with an independent interval -0.0417 to +0.0112 under the stricter validation threshold. The validation upper bound is below the approximate 10 percent clinical benchmark and the point estimate is opposite to the hypothesized stronger-dependency direction. Combining a null-to-small discovery estimate with a validation result that does not corroborate and fails to exclude the opposite or null pattern, the supplied dataset does not support a scientifically meaningful association between KRAS mutation and stronger KRAS dependency. Therefore H1 is rejected and closed. This rejection is limited to the supplied dataset and does not prove that KRAS mutation cannot matter in other contexts; it also leaves the pure MAPK-driver context H28 unresolved because excluding alternative MAPK drivers may still be biologically useful. The broader dataset conclusions now stand as follows. Supported strong dataset associations are SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high status with stronger WRN dependency, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss with stronger USP7 dependency, and KEAP1 loss with weaker, less negative NFE2L2 dependency. These are supported by very large absolute effects and narrow intervals. Context checks accepted adenocarcinoma specificity for SMARCA2, USP7, NFE2L2, and WRN, and accepted Avana-library robustness for SMARCA2. Negative or unsupported findings include broad BRAF V600E and EGFR amplification effects, EGFR amplification after validation, broad KRAS mutation after validation, MYC amplification effects on RPL11, POLR2A, and DHX9, ARID1A independent of SMARCA4 loss for SMARCA2 dependency, pure ERBB2 amplification on ERBB2 dependency, KRAS mutation on RIT1 dependency, and the original KEAP1-loss direction for stronger NFE2L2 dependency. Unresolved areas include broad ERBB2 amplification, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss for MDM2 dependency in broad and adenocarcinoma contexts, RB1 loss with KIF18A, BRCA2 loss with WRN, pure-context KRAS mutation, and several registered but untested context or biologically motivated comparisons. Next analyses should prioritize technical and biological robustness of the accepted large effects, including non-Avana library checks, lineage interactions, and the pure-context KRAS and BRAF refinements, before expanding into less coherent marker screens.

No discovery or validation assessments are due, so this explore stage registers new hypotheses that follow the strongest leads from iteration 2 rather than repeating completed tests. The accepted large dataset associations are still the highest-priority targets for context and technical robustness checks, because their magnitude far exceeds the approximate 10 percent relative benchmark and we now want to know whether they are diluted by lineage, library, or co-occurring DNA-repair contexts. I therefore add Avana-library robustness checks for WRN and USP7, an Avana-library check for the reversed KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 finding, and a BRCA2-intact restriction for MSI-high WRN to test whether the WRN association is not simply carried by BRCA2-loss cases. The previously registered non-Avana checks for SMARCA2, USP7, and NFE2L2 complement these. I also add adenocarcinoma-restricted KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency because broad and validation KRAS evidence was null or opposite, but a lineage-specific context could still matter. For the unresolved p53/MDM2 question, I register Avana and non-Avana library restrictions plus a lineage interaction because broad and adenocarcinoma estimates are small and imprecise; these checks may reveal whether the weak TP53 wild-type effect is context-specific or essentially absent. For broader biologically motivated exploration, I add MTAP loss versus SMARCA2 dependency in SMARCA4-intact cells as a co-deletion/chromatin-metabolic marker follow-up to the null ARID1A result, PIK3CA mutation versus STAT3 dependency as a PI3K-AKT-STAT3 signaling hypothesis, and ERBB2 amplification versus TMED10 dependency as a receptor-tyrosine kinase trafficking/secretory-pathway hypothesis. Direction coding follows the task convention: for mean differences, direction -1 means a positive signed estimate corresponds to a more negative, stronger dependency score in the exposed group relative to comparator, while direction +1 means a positive signed estimate corresponds to a less negative, weaker dependency score; interaction claims use the same signed-direction convention for the raw contrast. These proposals remain dataset associations and do not assume causality or external generalizability.

No evidence assessments are currently due, so this analyze stage requests 12 already-registered analyses that can materially update the strongest dataset conclusions and begin resolving the unresolved TP53/MDM2 question. First, I selected the missing library-robustness checks for the accepted large effects: H34 for SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 in non-Avana libraries, H37 for TP53 wild-type/USP7 in non-Avana libraries, H38 for KEAP1-loss/weaker NFE2L2 in non-Avana libraries, H43 for MSI-high/WRN in Avana libraries, H45 for TP53 wild-type/USP7 in Avana libraries, and H46 for KEAP1-loss/weaker NFE2L2 in Avana libraries. These absolute subgroup tests are more interpretable than interactions and test whether the very large effects are driven by the dominant Avana library or remain in the smaller non-Avana context. Second, I selected H44, MSI-high/WRN among BRCA2-intact cells, because WRN biology is connected to DNA repair and I want to know whether the accepted MSI-high association is not simply carried by overlapping BRCA2-loss cases. Third, I selected interaction tests H14, H15, H35, and H36 to evaluate whether adenocarcinoma versus non-adenocarcinoma lineage changes the SMARCA2, USP7, NFE2L2, and WRN associations. These interactions are secondary to the absolute subgroup tests but useful because a large absolute effect can still be heterogeneous across lineage subtypes. Fourth, I selected H40, TP53 wild-type versus TP53-loss for MDM2 dependency in the Avana library, because MDM2 remains unresolved and Avana provides the largest cell counts for a first focused resolution. I deliberately deferred broad ARID1A/SMARCA2 because the more specific ARID1A-in-SMARCA4-intact test was null, deferred pure BRAF because the broad claim was negative, and deferred new marker-outcome hypotheses such as MTAP/SMARCA2, PIK3CA/STAT3, KRAS/adenocarcinoma, and receptor-tyrosine-kinase/TMED10 hypotheses until the accepted-effects robustness set is resolved. All requested effects will be interpreted as associations within this supplied dataset, not as causal or broadly generalizable claims.

All newly delivered discovery estimates are valid under the cell-count rule and are interpreted using the sign conventions attached to each registered claim. For the direction -1 claims, a positive signed estimate means stronger, more negative dependency in the exposed or TP53 wild-type group; for the direction +1 NFE2L2 claims, a positive signed estimate means weaker, less negative NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1-loss cells. H34, H37, H38, H43, H45, H46, and H44 all show effects near +0.77 to +0.81 with lower bounds still far above any plausible 10% benchmark or absolute dependency-scale benchmark. These accept the context-specific extensions of the already supported major associations: SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 remains in non-Avana libraries, TP53 wild-type/USP7 remains in both Avana and non-Avana libraries, KEAP1-loss/weaker NFE2L2 remains in both library contexts, MSI-high/WRN remains in Avana libraries, and the MSI-high/WRN association remains essentially unchanged when BRCA2-loss cells are excluded. Although some non-Avana cells are smaller, they satisfy the 20-observation requirement and the intervals are still decisively large. I close these context checks because they have resolved the specific technical or co-occurring-marker robustness questions. The lineage interactions H14, H15, H35, and H36 are all near zero relative to their corresponding main effects, which are approximately 0.78. Their point estimates range from about -0.010 to -0.028 and their 95% intervals cross zero. This gives no positive evidence that adenocarcinoma versus non-adenocarcinoma context materially changes the accepted associations. However, because the intervals are wide enough to prevent a confident null-equivalence conclusion, especially for rare non-adenocarcinoma MSI-high cells, I leave these interaction claims unresolved but defer further investigation. H40, the Avana-library MDM2 TP53 wild-type comparison, is small and imprecise: signed estimate +0.013 with interval -0.013 to +0.039. With dependency_MDM2 mean around -0.27, a rough 10% absolute benchmark is about 0.027, so the point estimate is below the clinical benchmark and the interval includes both null and a possible small effect. I leave H40 active while waiting for H41 non-Avana MDM2 and H42 MDM2 lineage-interaction evidence. From a critical-review perspective, the very large accepted effects are not plausibly explained by multiple comparisons, and the context checks reduce the likelihood that they are artifacts of lineage or library distribution. They remain dataset associations, not causal claims. I am not requesting validation now because the accepted effects are already overwhelming across independent contexts, while the borderline small effects would likely be difficult to settle with one strict independent validation unless additional discovery contexts show a consistent near-threshold pattern.

Synthesis of due validation: H3 broad EGFR amplification versus stronger EGFR dependency now has independent validation. The hypothesis direction is -1, so a positive signed estimate means EGFR-amplified cells have more negative, stronger EGFR dependency. Discovery R3 was borderline: signed estimate +0.0252 with 95 percent interval -0.0003 to +0.0507. Using the overall dependency_EGFR mean around -0.2495, a 10 percent relative benchmark is about 0.025 dependency units, so the discovery estimate was only marginally above that benchmark and its interval included null. Independent validation R13 was opposite, signed estimate -0.0070 with a stricter independent interval -0.0487 to +0.0347. Although the validation upper bound still crosses the approximate clinical benchmark, the independent point estimate does not corroborate the hypothesized stronger-dependency direction and is small in the opposite direction. Combining a borderline discovery result with a non-replicating, opposite validation estimate, the supplied dataset does not support a scientifically meaningful positive association between EGFR amplification and stronger EGFR dependency. H3 therefore remains rejected and closed as a supported dataset claim. This rejection is not a proof that EGFR amplification never affects EGFR dependency in other datasets or contexts, but it removes support for the broad EGFR-amplification claim in this dataset. H24 adenocarcinoma SMARCA4 loss versus stronger SMARCA2 dependency is independently validated. Discovery R14 was signed +0.777 with interval +0.755 to +0.799; validation R39 was signed +0.816 with a much stricter interval +0.780 to +0.852. Both are vastly larger than the roughly 10 percent benchmark implied by the SMARCA2 mean around -0.415, which is about 0.042 dependency units. H24 is accepted and closed. This strongly corroborates the broad SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association and shows that the association is robust in the adenocarcinoma context. The main supported dataset conclusions are now: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, with broad, adenocarcinoma-specific, Avana-library, non-Avana-library, and independent validation support; MSI-high status is associated with much stronger WRN dependency, with broad, adenocarcinoma, Avana-library, and BRCA2-intact support; TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss is associated with much stronger USP7 dependency, with broad, adenocarcinoma, Avana-library, and non-Avana-library support; and KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker, less negative NFE2L2 dependency, with broad, adenocarcinoma, Avana-library, and non-Avana-library support. Major negative or unsupported claims remain: broad KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency, broad BRAF V600E versus BRAF dependency, EGFR amplification versus EGFR dependency, MYC amplification effects on RPL11, POLR2A, and DHX9, KRAS mutation versus RIT1 dependency, pure ERBB2 amplification versus ERBB2 dependency, ARID1A loss independent of SMARCA4 loss versus SMARCA2 dependency, and the original KEAP1-loss direction for stronger NFE2L2 dependency. Unresolved areas include broad ERBB2 amplification, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss for MDM2 dependency across broad, adenocarcinoma, and library contexts, RB1 loss versus KIF18A, BRCA2 loss versus WRN, pure-context KRAS mutation, pure-context BRAF, lineage interactions for the large effects, and several registered but untested biologically motivated marker-outcome comparisons. The most informative next analyses are to complete the TP53/MDM2 context set with H41 and H42, then test driver-context refinements such as H39 adenocarcinoma KRAS and H29 pure-context BRAF, and then proceed to broader marker screens such as H47 MTAP/SMARCA2, H48 PIK3CA/STAT3, H49 ERBB2/TMED10, and remaining active untested outcome-marker hypotheses. Independent validation is best conserved for borderline or context-specific claims after discovery contexts show consistent near-threshold signals, rather than spending more validation on the already overwhelming large effects.

No discovery or validation assessments are due, so this explore stage registers corrected and additional scientific follow-ups while avoiding the previous invalid variable name. The earlier attempt used cdn2a_loss; the correct schema variable is cdkn2a_loss, and all proposals below use valid public variables only. The main accepted effects are already strongly supported across broad, adenocarcinoma, Avana, non-Avana, and related contexts, so the priority now is to resolve borderline small effects and test biologically coherent context modifications rather than re-testing huge accepted effects. First, I refine the unresolved TP53-to-MDM2 question. Broad, adenocarcinoma, Avana, and pending non-Avana or lineage interaction tests have not yet produced a clear MDM2 signal near the roughly 0.027 absolute benchmark implied by a 10 percent relative effect on mean dependency_MDM2 about -0.269. I register TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss within CDKN2A-intact cells, because CDKN2A loss may dilute or reshape p53-MDM2 pathway dependence, and I test CDKN2A loss versus intact within TP53 wild-type cells to see whether the CDKN2A/p14ARF axis directly modifies MDM2 dependency among nominally p53-functional lines. Second, I follow the accepted strong TP53 wild-type-to-USP7 association by testing CDKN2A loss within TP53 wild-type cells. If CDKN2A loss reduces p53-pathway dependence, USP7 dependency should be weaker, which is coded as direction +1 and expected raw positive exposed-minus-comparator. Third, I test PTEN loss versus STAT3 dependency broadly and among PIK3CA wild-type cells, motivated by PI3K pathway alteration and STAT3 signaling. For direction -1 claims, stronger dependency in the exposed group corresponds to raw negative exposed-minus-comparator and is reported as positive after direction signing. Fourth, I refine SMARCA2 by testing whether the very large SMARCA4-loss effect is further modified by co-occurring ARID1A loss or MTAP loss among SMARCA4-loss cells. These are not tests of independent chromatin loss in SMARCA4-intact cells, which were already negative; they test whether co-alterations deepen or modify an already established context. Fifth, I add MAPK-pathway context tests: NF1 loss versus KRAS dependency and NF1 loss versus BRAF dependency. NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling; it may be associated with stronger KRAS dependency but weaker BRAF dependency if alternative MAPK activation reduces dependence on BRAF specifically. Sixth, I add STK11 loss versus NFE2L2 dependency with uncertain direction, because oxidative-stress and metabolic stress pathways may overlap with KEAP1-NFE2L2 biology, and APC mutation versus TMED10 dependency as a Wnt-secretion trafficking screen. Seventh, I refine the broad null-to-small RB1-KIF18A result within adenocarcinoma. All proposals are associations within this supplied dataset, not causal claims or claims about external generalizability.

No assessments are due, so I request twelve already registered analyses. The first priority is to finish resolving the weak, unresolved TP53-to-MDM2 association. Broad and Avana estimates have been small and imprecise, so I test the complementary non-Avana library context (H41), the adenocarcinoma-versus-non-adenocarcinoma interaction (H42), a CDKN2A-intact restriction (H50), and a direct CDKN2A-loss effect within TP53 wild-type cells (H51). CDKN2A is biologically relevant to p53 pathway integrity through ARF-MDM2, so these tests distinguish whether the weak broad signal is diluted by co-loss or is simply near null. Second, I broaden to mechanistically motivated marker-outcome hypotheses that have not been tested. PI3K pathway alteration could modify STAT3 dependency, so I run PIK3CA mutation versus STAT3 (H48), PTEN loss versus STAT3 broadly (H53), and PTEN loss versus STAT3 within PIK3CA wild-type cells (H54). Third, MAPK biology is tested with NF1 loss: direction -1 for KRAS, expecting stronger KRAS dependency if RAS pathway activation increases dependence on KRAS, and direction +1 for BRAF, expecting weaker BRAF dependency if NF1 loss provides alternative MAPK activation or bypasses BRAF. Fourth, I add secretory-pathway and oxidative-stress screens: ERBB2 amplification versus TMED10 (H49), APC mutation versus TMED10 (H60), and STK11 loss versus NFE2L2 with direction +1, which tests weaker NFE2L2 dependency as the primary direction. These choices avoid repeatedly testing the already robust large effects unless they are direct co-alteration refinements, and they prioritize the remaining borderline MDM2 context plus high-value new associations. All estimates will be assessed as associations in the supplied dataset, not as causal or externally generalizable claims.

All due discovery results are valid cell-count-wise and are interpreted using the signed hypothesis directions. The strongest new finding is PTEN loss versus STAT3 dependency. H53 has signed estimate +0.267 with interval +0.215 to +0.319, and H54, restricted to PIK3CA wild-type cells, has signed estimate +0.267 with interval +0.210 to +0.323. For direction -1, positive signed values mean PTEN-loss cells have more negative, stronger STAT3 dependency. Using the dependency_STAT3 mean around -0.282, a 10% benchmark is about 0.028, so both intervals are far above that threshold and the effect is not plausibly a multiplicity artifact or a PIK3CA co-alteration confound in this dataset. I accept H53 and H54, and I request independent validation of the more specific PIK3CA wild-type refinement H54. PIK3CA mutation versus STAT3 (H48) showed no evidence for the hypothesized stronger dependency and its signed upper bound is below the approximate clinical benchmark, so it is rejected and closed. NF1-loss associations are not supportive of the hypothesized directions: H57 rejects stronger KRAS dependency and H58 is unresolved for weaker BRAF dependency because the interval crosses zero and still admits a possible meaningful positive effect. H49 and H60 are near-null TMED10 screens and are deferred because their intervals are not precise enough to rule out modest positive effects. H59 is also deferred because STK11 loss gives a small opposite point estimate with a wide interval. I reassessed the two due validation items and the reversed CDKN2A-MDM2 claim. H1 broad KRAS mutation versus stronger KRAS dependency remains unsupported. The original discovery was small and null (signed estimate +0.014; interval crossed zero), and the independent validation is small and in the opposite direction (signed estimate -0.015; independent interval -0.042 to +0.011). The validation upper bound is also below the approximate 10% absolute benchmark of about 0.024 for dependency_KRAS mean about -0.245. H54, PTEN loss versus stronger STAT3 dependency in PIK3CA wild-type cells, is independently validated. The discovery estimate was signed +0.267 [0.210, 0.323], and validation R52 was larger: signed +0.325 [0.239, 0.412]. Current supported main findings are SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high status with much stronger WRN dependency, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss with much stronger USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, PTEN loss with much stronger STAT3 dependency, and CDKN2A loss with much stronger MDM2 dependency in TP53 wild-type cells. Key negative findings include broad KRAS-mutant KRAS dependency, broad BRAF V600E dependency, EGFR amplification dependency, MYC amplification effects on RPL11/POLR2A/DHX9, PIK3CA mutation versus STAT3, and NF1 loss versus stronger KRAS dependency. Unresolved areas remain broad ERBB2 amplification, broad TP53 wild-type versus MDM2, RB1/KIF18A, pure driver contexts, lineage interactions, USP7 CDKN2A context, NF1/BRAF direction, and SMARCA2 co-alteration contexts. Next analysis should prioritize the registered MDM2 CDKN2A contexts and PTEN/STAT3 contexts, plus already active co-loss and pure-context claims.

No validation or discovery assessments are due. I registered follow-ups that serve three purposes. First, I test whether the newly accepted or strongly supported associations are context-dependent rather than uniformly present: PTEN loss and stronger STAT3 dependency in high IFN-gamma signature, SMARCA4 loss and stronger SMARCA2 dependency in high EMT score, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss and stronger USP7 dependency in high stemness score, and KEAP1 loss and weaker NFE2L2 dependency in high hypoxia score. These are interaction contrasts, so a positive signed value means the hypothesized association is stronger in the named high-score subgroup than in its complement within the same eligible population. This is scientifically useful because these scores are measured phenotypic contexts, not causal assignments. Second, I test technical and marker contexts for robustness and possible confounding: the CDKN2A-loss effect on MDM2 among TP53 wild-type cells within research_marker_d_positive, and PTEN loss and STAT3 dependency within screen_batch batch_a. Third, I add new marker-outcome comparisons: NF1 loss versus RIT1 dependency, because NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK signaling and RIT1 is a RAS-related gene; PIK3CA mutation versus ERBB2 dependency in the downstream-bypass direction; MTAP loss versus MDM2 dependency among TP53 wild-type and CDKN2A-intact cells, to ask whether another locus co-deletion marker is independently associated with MDM2 dependency; and research_marker_d_positive versus STAT3 dependency, because marker D is a constructed binary assay and may act as a negative control or potential confounder if it is associated with the same outcome. These remain exploratory associations in the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

No discovery or validation assessments are due, so this analysis stage is used to request the highest-value untested registered comparisons. All twelve newly delivered discovery results have valid comparison cells. I used the same approximate 10% absolute benchmark relative to the outcome mean magnitude, e.g. about 0.027 for dependency_MDM2, 0.028 for dependency_STAT3, 0.042 for dependency_SMARCA2, and about 0.01-0.026 for smaller-mean outcomes, while also weighing uncertainty and cell sizes. The CDKN2A-loss/MDM2 association among TP53 wild-type cells remains robust in several contexts: adenocarcinoma H63 gave signed +0.103 [0.057,0.148], Avana H64 gave +0.117 [0.074,0.160], and research_marker_D-positive cells H73 gave +0.110 [0.056,0.164]. Every lower bound exceeds the approximate MDM2 benchmark, so these are accepted context checks supporting H62 rather than explanations of the effect away. PTEN loss also remains associated with much stronger STAT3 dependency within screen_batch batch_a, H74: +0.234 [0.125,0.342], accepted and closed. The phenotype-signature interaction hypotheses H69-H72 are unresolved and deferred: H69 has a positive but extremely imprecise interaction with high IFN-gamma signature (+0.083 [-0.091,0.257]) and only 26 exposed high-IFN lines; H70 is near null (+0.010 [-0.056,0.076]); H71 and H72 have negative point estimates but upper bounds still permit meaningful interactions in the registered directions. Thus I do not accept any clinically meaningful effect modification by IFN-gamma, EMT, stemness, or hypoxia. H24 asks whether SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency among adenocarcinoma cells in this lung line dataset. The discovery estimate was signed +0.777 [0.755, 0.799] and the independent validation was even larger, +0.816 [0.780, 0.852]. Using the absolute mean dependency_SMARCA2 magnitude around 0.415, a 10% benchmark is about 0.042; the validation lower bound is an order of magnitude above that. Therefore I accept H24 and close it. This strengthens the main supported dataset association: SMARCA4 loss is associated with markedly stronger SMARCA2 dependency, and that association is not confined to the broad population but is also robust within adenocarcinoma. The finding is an association in the supplied CRISPR screen dataset, not a causal statement or a claim about external generalizability. Current supported dataset associations include SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss with much stronger USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, PTEN loss with much stronger STAT3 dependency, and CDKN2A loss with much stronger MDM2 dependency among TP53 wild-type cells. Key negative or non-supported claims include broad KRAS mutation for KRAS dependency, broad BRAF V600E for BRAF dependency, EGFR amplification for EGFR dependency, MYC amplification effects on RPL11/POLR2A/DHX9, PIK3CA mutation for weaker ERBB2 or stronger STAT3, NF1 loss for stronger KRAS dependency, and NF1 loss for stronger RIT1 dependency. Remaining uncertainty includes whether accepted effects depend on measured phenotypic contexts, whether MTAP or other co-deletions confound CDKN2A-MDM2, whether PTEN-STAT3 and SMARCA4-SMARCA2 persist in additional molecular and technical contexts, and whether unresolved pure-driver or subtype-specific comparisons reveal heterogeneity. The next most informative analyses should test specificity and robustness: H65 CDKN2A loss in TP53-loss cells to test MDM2 context dependence, H66-H68 PTEN loss STAT3 contexts, H80 CDKN2A loss in marker-D-negative cells, H79 the reversed NF1/RIT1 direction, H52 USP7/CDKN2A among TP53 wild-type cells, SMARCA2 co-loss claims, pure-driver KRAS/BRAF contexts, and RB1/KIF18A. The newly registered MTAP-intact CDKN2A-MDM2 claim should also be evaluated because it may help separate locus-specific CDKN2A association from broader 9p21 co-deletion confounding.

No validation or discovery assessments are due. I registered twelve new or parent-linked hypotheses for later discovery analysis. The first eight test whether accepted associations remain present after changing or restricting context, which helps separate robust dataset associations from co-alteration or technical artifacts. Broad CDKN2A loss is tested for MDM2 dependency to determine whether the TP53-wild-type restriction changes the overall estimate. The USP7 association with TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss is tested separately within CDKN2A-loss and CDKN2A-intact cells to determine whether the strong USP7 effect is intrinsic to p53 state or confounded by 9p21/CDKN2A co-loss. MDM2 is also tested reciprocally: among CDKN2A-loss cells, does TP53 wild-type versus loss still imply stronger MDM2 dependency? Accepted SMARCA4-SMARCA2, KEAP1-NFE2L2, and PTEN-STAT3 associations are tested in DNA-complete lines to check robustness across an omics-completeness context. CDKN2A-loss/MDM2 in TP53-wild-type DNA-complete cells is added as a more targeted robustness check. Finally, I add pathway cross-talk hypotheses: KRAS mutation should be associated with weaker EGFR dependency if downstream KRAS activation bypasses EGFR; EGFR amplification may imply stronger KRAS dependency if upstream receptor activation increases pathway reliance; NF1 loss is tested in the reversed direction against KRAS dependency because prior NF1-loss/KRAS evidence favored the opposite of the originally registered direction; and EGFR amplification is tested against ERBB2 dependency as an additional RTK-pathway relationship. These comparisons remain discovery associations in the supplied dataset; acceptance or rejection will depend on effect magnitude, uncertainty, and cell counts.

No discovery or validation assessments are due, so this stage requests the highest-value untested comparisons. The first priority is specificity of the accepted USP7 and MDM2 associations. For USP7, H83 and H84 ask whether TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss remains associated with stronger USP7 dependency within CDKN2A-loss and CDKN2A-intact contexts, while H52 asks whether CDKN2A loss has an independent association with USP7 dependency among TP53 wild-type cells. Together these separate a genuine p53-state association from 9p21/CDKN2A co-alteration confounding. For MDM2, H85 tests the reciprocal context: TP53 wild-type versus loss among CDKN2A-loss cells. H65 tests CDKN2A loss among TP53-loss cells, which should be weak or null if the accepted CDKN2A/MDM2 effect is TP53-wild-type-specific. H82 tests the unrestricted CDKN2A/MDM2 association, showing how much attenuation occurs when TP53 wild-type cells are mixed with TP53-loss cells. H81 and H80 test whether the accepted CDKN2A/MDM2 association persists after excluding MTAP co-deletion contexts or in research-marker-D-negative cells, helping distinguish locus-specific CDKN2A association from co-deletion or constructed-marker confounding. The second priority is completing technical/subtype robustness for PTEN/STAT3: H66 restricts to Avana-library screens and H68 restricts to adenocarcinoma, the two major contexts where most other accepted associations have been checked. The third priority adds focused RTK/RAS cross-talk breadth: H90 tests KRAS mutation versus EGFR dependency, where downstream KRAS activation may bypass EGFR, and H91 tests EGFR amplification versus KRAS dependency, where upstream receptor activation may increase pathway reliance. I omitted H86 and H89 as lower-value DNA-complete robustness checks for KEAP1 and SMARCA4 because those associations already have multiple subtype, library, or validation checks. I omitted H87 because H66/H68 are more informative contexts for PTEN. I omitted H92 because it reuses existing NF1-loss KRAS evidence and gives no new sample. No conclusion is drawn before the analyses arrive; all requests remain discovery associations in the supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable claims.

All twelve newly delivered results have valid comparison cells and are signed to the registered hypothesis direction. I judged them against the approximate 10% clinical-significance benchmark in absolute dependency-score units: roughly 0.009 for USP7, 0.027 for MDM2, 0.028 for STAT3, 0.025 for EGFR, and 0.025 for KRAS. The USP7 context tests H83 and H84 are both overwhelmingly supportive: TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss is associated with much stronger USP7 dependency within CDKN2A-loss lines, +0.808 [0.767,0.849], and within CDKN2A-intact lines, +0.800 [0.778,0.823]. Because both lower bounds exceed the benchmark by two orders of magnitude, I accept and close them. This strongly argues that the accepted USP7-p53 association is not explained away by CDKN2A co-deletion. H52 tested whether CDKN2A loss has an independent association with USP7 dependency among TP53 wild-type cells. The signed estimate was near zero and opposite to the registered direction, -0.0028 [-0.025,0.020]; the upper bound still permits a small positive association above benchmark, so I leave it unresolved but deferred because it is not central after H83/H84. For MDM2, H82 accepts the broad CDKN2A-loss association, +0.117 [0.082,0.152], and H65 accepts the same direction among TP53-loss lines, +0.111 [0.035,0.186], with both lower bounds above the MDM2 benchmark. Together with the accepted TP53 wild-type-restricted claim H62 and the adenocarcinoma/Avana context checks, these results broaden the MDM2 association from being merely TP53-wild-type-restricted to a dataset association with CDKN2A loss across p53 states. H81 accepts the association when TP53 wild-type and MTAP-loss are excluded, +0.106 [0.063,0.150], and H80 accepts it among TP53 wild-type, marker-D-negative cells, +0.125 [0.069,0.182], further arguing against MTAP co-deletion or constructed-marker confounding. The reciprocal H85 tests whether TP53 wild-type versus loss remains associated with stronger MDM2 dependency within CDKN2A-loss lines; the estimate is small and very imprecise, +0.015 [-0.067,0.097]. It does not support a large TP53 effect in that stratum, but the upper bound still exceeds benchmark, so it remains unresolved and deferred. Together with the broad near-null TP53 effect and H50's imprecise CDKN2A-intact stratum result, the evidence pattern favors CDKN2A loss as the better predictor of MDM2 dependency in this dataset. PTEN loss remains strongly associated with much stronger STAT3 dependency in both major untested robustness contexts: Avana-library screens, +0.288 [0.232,0.343], and adenocarcinoma subtype, +0.268 [0.206,0.330]. I accept and close both. H90 rejects the registered hypothesis that KRAS mutation is associated with weaker EGFR dependency: the signed positive-direction interval is near null/negative, -0.010 [-0.027,0.008], and its upper bound is below the EGFR benchmark. H91 remains unresolved because EGFR amplification could still be associated with stronger KRAS dependency, +0.009 [-0.018,0.037], although the point estimate is small. I requested independent validation for H82 because it upgrades the MDM2 conclusion from a TP53-wild-type-restricted association to a broad dataset association, making reproducibility of this primary claim the most valuable validation target. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

The new validation evidence strengthens the two primary accepted associations it addresses. H54 tests PTEN loss versus dependency_STAT3 among PIK3CA-mutation-negative lines. The discovery signed estimate was +0.267 [0.210,0.323], and independent validation was larger, +0.325 [0.239,0.412]. With a dependency_STAT3 clinical benchmark near 0.028, both intervals are far above that threshold; the validation interval does not overlap the discovery interval but still supports a very large positive signed effect. I therefore accept H54 and close it. This further consolidates the accepted dataset association that PTEN loss is associated with much stronger STAT3 dependency, robust across the PIK3CA-wild-type restriction and independent validation. H82 tests the broad CDKN2A-loss versus dependency_MDM2 association without restricting to TP53 state. Discovery was +0.117 [0.082,0.152] and independent validation was essentially the same, +0.118 [0.069,0.166]. The validation lower bound remains well above the approximate MDM2 benchmark of 0.027, so I accept and close H82. This is important because it converts the MDM2 conclusion from an association limited to TP53-wild-type contexts into a broad dataset association with CDKN2A loss. Combined with H65 among TP53-loss cells, H63/H64 context checks, H80 marker-D-negative stratum, and H81 MTAP-intact stratum, the most parsimonious supported interpretation in this dataset is that CDKN2A loss is the primary predictor of stronger MDM2 dependency, while broad TP53 loss alone is not clearly predictive. H57 tests the originally registered direction that NF1 loss would be associated with stronger dependency_KRAS. The discovery signed estimate favored the opposite direction, and the new validation signed estimate was also negative, -0.009 [-0.047,0.030]. Although the independent interval is wide enough to admit an expected-direction effect at its upper edge, the point estimate is near zero and opposite to H57, and the prior discovery point estimate was also opposite. The evidence does not support a clinically meaningful NF1-loss association in the registered H57 direction, so I reject and close it. H92, the complementary positive-direction claim, remains unresolved: both raw point estimates point in the H92 direction, but the validation point estimate is only +0.009 and the interval is wide, with upper bound above the KRAS benchmark. I do not accept H92, but I also do not fully reject it because meaningful positive effects remain possible within uncertainty. Since this has now been independently validated and the point is small, I deprioritize it as deferred. Current supported associations remain SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency, TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss with much stronger USP7 dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, PTEN loss with much stronger STAT3 dependency, and now independently supported CDKN2A loss with much stronger MDM2 dependency across p53 states. Next analyses should focus on remaining active specificity/robustness items: PTEN/STAT3 in non-Avana screens, SMARCA2 co-loss or co-deletion contexts, pure-driver KRAS/BRAF/EGFR/ERBB2 comparisons, RB1/KIF18A subtype-specific tests, and DNA-complete checks. I did not request additional validation because H82 and H54 were just validated and are settled; remaining high-value items are mostly untested contexts or lower-priority unresolved interactions.

No assessments are due. I registered twelve falsifiable follow-up comparisons. First, I registered refinements of accepted associations that test whether they persist in co-alteration contexts that could confound them: SMARCA4-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency within MTAP-loss cells, TP53-wild-type versus TP53-loss USP7 dependency within MTAP-loss cells, KEAP1-loss versus NFE2L2 dependency within STK11-loss cells, PTEN-loss versus STAT3 dependency in PIK3CA-mutant cells, MSI-high versus WRN dependency among higher-mutation-burden lines, CDKN2A-loss versus MDM2 dependency among PTEN-loss cells, and PTEN-loss versus STAT3 dependency within KEAP1-loss or CDKN2A-loss strata. These comparisons distinguish pathway/locus-specific dataset associations from broad co-deletion or co-alteration patterns. Second, I added a genomic-instability hypothesis for WRN: among MSI-negative lines, higher mutation burden should be associated with stronger WRN dependency if the WRN signal reflects genome instability rather than MSI status alone. Third, I added RTK/RAS cross-talk tests with explicit expected directions: KRAS mutation may weaken upstream ERBB2 dependency, ERBB2 amplification may strengthen KRAS dependency, and EGFR amplification may alter RIT1 dependency if upstream receptor activation feeds RAS-family signaling. All proposals remain exploratory associations in the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims.

No discovery or validation assessments are due. I request the twelve newly registered analyses because they directly address the highest-priority scientific questions from the current ledger. The first group tests context specificity of major accepted associations: H94 tests SMARCA4 loss within MTAP-loss cells; H95 tests the TP53 wild-type versus loss USP7 contrast within MTAP-loss cells; H96 tests KEAP1 loss within STK11-loss cells; H97 tests PTEN loss within PIK3CA-mutant cells; H100 tests CDKN2A loss within PTEN-loss cells; and H101/H102 test PTEN loss within KEAP1-loss or CDKN2A-loss contexts. These are important because many accepted effects are large, and the key issue now is whether they persist in co-alteration settings rather than being artifacts of linked genomic events or pathway confounding. H98 and H99 test WRN biology beyond the accepted MSI-high contrast: whether MSI-high remains meaningful among higher mutation burden and whether mutation burden itself predicts stronger WRN dependency among MSI-negative lines. The last group adds focused RTK/RAS cross-talk breadth: H103 tests KRAS mutation with ERBB2 dependency, H104 tests ERBB2 amplification with KRAS dependency, and H105 tests EGFR amplification with RIT1 dependency. These comparisons are all new or untested in the supplied ledger, and each uses either a binary exposure or a numeric exposure contrast that should be adequately powered given the global prevalence of the predictor and the overall n=2000. No conclusions are being drawn before the analyses arrive.

I assessed all newly delivered discovery evidence using approximate 10% clinical-significance benchmarks derived from the global absolute scale of each dependency score: about 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.009 for USP7 and NFE2L2, 0.028 for STAT3, 0.030 for WRN, 0.027 for MDM2, 0.026 for ERBB2 and RIT1, and 0.024-0.025 for KRAS. The major co-alteration specificity tests are strong. H94 shows that within MTAP-loss lines, SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, +0.779 [0.733,0.825], far above the benchmark and with small cells that are still valid. This argues against treating the accepted SMARCA4/SMARCA2 association as merely an MTAP co-deletion artifact. H95 similarly shows TP53-wild-type versus TP53-loss remains associated with much stronger USP7 dependency within MTAP-loss lines, +0.766 [0.719,0.813]. H96 shows the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association persists among STK11-loss lines, +0.775 [0.727,0.823]. For PTEN/STAT3, H97, H101, and H102 show the association persists within PIK3CA-mutant, KEAP1-loss, and CDKN2A-loss strata: +0.268 [0.127,0.409], +0.247 [0.133,0.361], and +0.252 [0.130,0.373], respectively. All lower bounds exceed the STAT3 benchmark. H98 shows MSI-high remains associated with much stronger WRN dependency among higher-mutation-burden lines, +0.780 [0.750,0.811]. Therefore H94-H98, H101, and H102 are accepted and closed. H100 is different: the PTEN-loss subgroup gives CDKN2A loss associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, +0.125 [0.029,0.221], with only 51 CDKN2A-loss cells. The point estimate is clinically meaningful and consistent with the validated broad CDKN2A/MDM2 association, but the lower bound is barely above the approximate MDM2 benchmark and the subgroup is small. I leave it unresolved and active and request independent validation because confirmation or attenuation in this PTEN-loss co-context is the most informative next decision. H103 rejects the hypothesis that KRAS mutation is associated with stronger ERBB2 dependency: the signed interval is centered near zero, -0.0009 [-0.0180,0.0162], and the upper bound is below the ERBB2 benchmark. H104 and H105 are unresolved but deferred: their point estimates are near null, although their upper bounds remain compatible with modest positive signed associations for ERBB2 amplification with KRAS dependency and EGFR amplification with RIT1 dependency. H99 failed to produce a valid estimate because the requested numeric mutation-burden contrast yielded insufficient comparison cells. This is not evidence of no association, but the specific specification is untestable as written, so I mark it unresolved and close that specification. I did not register a parented refinement here because the invalid H99 result itself provides no motivating evidence; the scientific question can be pursued later through binary stratified specifications. All conclusions remain dataset associations and do not establish causality or generalizability.

The new validation for H100 is consistent in point estimate but too imprecise to confirm the PTEN-loss subgroup effect. Discovery showed CDKN2A-loss lines, compared with CDKN2A-intact lines, having stronger dependency_MDM2 within PTEN-loss cells: signed effect +0.125 [0.029, 0.221], close to but just above the approximate MDM2 clinical benchmark near 0.027. Independent validation gave +0.111 [-0.026, 0.248]. The validation point estimate is clinically meaningful and in the same direction, but the 99.6% interval crosses zero and its lower bound is below both null and the approximate benchmark. With only 61 validation CDKN2A-loss cells, this small co-alteration stratum remains uncertain. I therefore keep H100 unresolved and deprioritize it as deferred. This does not weaken the primary CDKN2A-loss association with dependency_MDM2, which is accepted and independently validated broadly in H82 and supported across several TP53-state and co-alteration contexts. More broadly, the supported dataset associations are: SMARCA4 loss with much stronger dependency_SMARCA2, including MTAP-loss contexts; TP53 wild-type versus TP53 loss with much stronger dependency_USP7, including CDKN2A-loss and MTAP-loss contexts; KEAP1 loss with weaker dependency_NFE2L2, including STK11-loss contexts; MSI-high with much stronger dependency_WRN, including Avana, adenocarcinoma, BRCA2-intact, and higher-mutation-burden contexts; PTEN loss with much stronger dependency_STAT3, including PIK3CA-wild-type, PIK3CA-mutant, KEAP1-loss, CDKN2A-loss, Avana, and adenocarcinoma contexts; and CDKN2A loss with much stronger dependency_MDM2, including TP53-wild-type, TP53-loss, MTAP-intact, marker-D-negative, Avana, and adenocarcinoma contexts. Major negative or non-supported findings include broad KRAS-mutation, BRAF-V600E, EGFR-amplification, and broad ERBB2 amplification associations with their own driver dependencies in the expected direction; MYC amplification with RPL11, POLR2A, or DHX9 dependency; broad NF1-loss with dependency_KRAS in the registered direction; KRAS mutation with stronger dependency_ERBB2; and PTEN-independent PIK3CA mutation with stronger dependency_STAT3. Unresolved but low-priority areas include the PTEN-loss CDKN2A/MDM2 co-context, remaining RTK/RAS cross-talk near-null effects, broad TP53 effects on dependency_MDM2, and several untested robustness contexts. The next most informative analyses are the existing active DNA-complete checks H86-H89, pure-driver KRAS and BRAF comparisons H28/H29, PTEN-loss STAT3 in non-Avana screens H67, and SMARCA2 co-loss contexts H55/H56, plus the newly registered pure EGFR comparison and CDKN2A-loss MDM2 comparison in non-Avana screens. These test whether accepted associations persist under genomic completeness, driver purity, library variation, and additional co-loss settings. All statements remain associations in this supplied dataset and do not establish causality or external generalizability.

No assessments are due at this exploration stage. I registered twelve follow-up comparisons to sharpen the current evidence. First, I added robustness checks for accepted or partially robust associations: MSI-high versus dependency_WRN in Ky-library screens and in DNA-complete lines, and TP53-wild-type versus TP53-loss versus dependency_USP7 in DNA-complete lines. These test whether the WRN and USP7 signals persist under a different screen library and when DNA genomic calls are present. Second, I registered co-alteration specificity checks for the major accepted clusters: SMARCA4 loss versus dependency_SMARCA2 within KEAP1-loss lines, TP53 status versus dependency_USP7 within KEAP1-loss lines, KEAP1 loss versus dependency_NFE2L2 within TP53-loss lines, MSI-high versus dependency_WRN within TP53-loss lines, PTEN loss versus dependency_STAT3 within STK11-loss lines, and CDKN2A loss versus dependency_MDM2 within KEAP1-loss and STK11-loss lines. These are falsifiable context tests: if the associations remain large and signed in the expected direction, they are less likely to be artifacts of a single linked co-alteration or a narrow genomic context. If they collapse toward zero or fall below approximately 10% relative clinical benchmarks for the relevant dependency score, I would qualify the association as context-dependent. I used approximate outcome-specific benchmarks near 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.009 for USP7 and NFE2L2, 0.028 for STAT3, and 0.027 for MDM2. Third, I added two pure cross-driver KRAS/BRAF tests excluding EGFR and ERBB2 amplification: BRAF-V600E versus dependency_KRAS and KRAS mutation versus dependency_BRAF. Because driver-pathway activation can reduce dependency on an adjacent upstream or downstream kinase, I anticipated a positive signed contrast in these tests, meaning weaker dependency in the exposed driver-mutant group, but the broad driver-dependency nulls already observed make uncertainty high. All registered claims remain associations in this supplied dataset and do not establish causality or external generalizability.

No assessments are due, so I selected twelve active claims that should provide new evidence. I did not request several other active claims because they overlap with more informative contexts or have lower prior probability, such as pure EGFR or additional redundant co-alteration contexts. These analyses will produce discovery estimates and intervals already signed to the registered directions; no scientific conclusions should be drawn until appraise receives the results.

I assessed all newly delivered discovery evidence using approximate 10%-relative clinical benchmarks: about 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.009 for USP7 and NFE2L2, 0.028 for STAT3, 0.027 for MDM2, and 0.024-0.025 for KRAS/BRAF. The DNA-complete robustness checks are decisive: H86 gives KEAP1-loss associated with weaker dependency_NFE2L2 in DNA-complete lines, +0.797 [0.776,0.819]; H89 gives SMARCA4 loss associated with much stronger dependency_SMARCA2, +0.782 [0.761,0.802]; H109 gives MSI-high associated with much stronger dependency_WRN, +0.790 [0.760,0.820]; and H110 gives TP53-wild-type versus TP53-loss associated with much stronger dependency_USP7, +0.804 [0.783,0.825]. All lower bounds are far above the relevant benchmark, so H86, H89, H109, and H110 are accepted and closed. Screen-library robustness is also strong for H108, where MSI-high in Ky-library screens gives +0.732 [0.675,0.790], and for H107, where CDKN2A loss in non-Avana screens gives +0.125 [0.029,0.221]. H107 is small and its lower bound is only just above the MDM2 benchmark, but it is directionally consistent with the already validated broad CDKN2A/MDM2 association and excludes both null and clinical indifference at 95%, so I accept it as a dataset-level technical robustness result rather than a new biological effect. I did not request validation now: the newly accepted effects are either enormous and redundant with prior validated clusters or are small technical subgroup checks likely to remain imprecise, while the main unresolved cross-driver question is better addressed first by the refined driver-pure analyses. The new validation and deadline responses materially strengthen the primary association set while clarifying where subgroup effects remain imprecise. For H57, NF1 loss was hypothesized to be associated with stronger dependency_KRAS. The point estimates do not support stronger KRAS dependency after NF1 loss, so I keep this claim rejected and closed, while noting that the independent interval has a slight upper tail near the clinical scale; I do not promote the reverse NF1-to-weaker-KRAS hypothesis because both estimates remain too imprecise and small. For H102, PTEN loss within TP53-loss lines showed strong discovery evidence for stronger dependency_STAT3, signed +0.252 [0.130, 0.373]. Independent validation was directionally consistent and nonzero at the stringent interval, +0.205 [0.018, 0.393], but the lower bound fell below the approximate STAT3 benchmark of 0.028 because the TP53-loss/PTEN-loss intersection is small.
